title: CTO Interview with Taylor Barton of Certus Semiconductor
gist: In this interview, Certus Semiconductor engineer Taylor Barton says high bump counts in AI, automotive and HPC chips are pushing more die area into I/O. Certus sells custom, pruned I/O and ESD libraries plus compact array-able ADC/DAC IP as a smaller-area alternative to competitors' 'kitchen-sink' libraries. Barton also says advanced nodes limited to about 1.2V will still have to support legacy 1.8V and 3.3V protocols. The title calls Barton the CTO, but the text describes him as a Lead Analog/Mixed-Signal and I/O IC Design Engineer.

themes.theme: I/O area pressure from high bump counts

insights.claim: Chips for AI, automotive and high-performance computing need ever-higher bump counts, so a growing share of die area has to go to I/O. Chip-core engineers often treat this area as 'dead space' that raises production cost without adding processing power.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: As the I/O share of the die grows, I/O and ESD IP that saves area becomes a real cost lever in AI and HPC silicon.
insights.quote: chip-core engineers often see it as “dead space”, silicon area that consumes real estate and inflates production costs without directly adding core processing power

insights.claim: Certus Semiconductor argues that the large configurable 'kitchen-sink' I/O libraries from other industry leaders leave unused control logic and bloated footprints. In its view, area is cost, so these libraries are rarely the best fit for high-bump-count chips built for a specific application.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Niche IP vendors are positioning against generic I/O libraries from larger IP suppliers on die-area cost.
insights.quote: it doesn’t optimize for area, and in semiconductor manufacturing, area is cost
insights.locator: What other approaches are being used

themes.theme: Certus custom I/O and ESD approach

insights.claim: Certus Semiconductor tailors each I/O library to the customer. It analyzes power buses, ESD constraints and reliability parameters, then removes the features the customer does not need to increase density. It says its ESD structures routinely exceed industry-standard requirements while using less area.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This is a services-heavy, custom IP model that competes on area and integration fit rather than catalog breadth.

insights.so_what: This shows demand for custom I/O IP in both AI accelerators and automotive end markets.

insights.claim: Certus Semiconductor built a compact, array-able custom ADC and DAC solution for a customer that needed a large array of converters on one chip. Both blocks beat the customer's performance spec, came in under its area target and are now silicon proven.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This marks Certus's move from I/O into analog converter IP, which widens its addressable market.

insights.claim: Future I/O libraries will increasingly be built at low single-digit-nanometer nodes, where transistors are natively limited to about 1.2V I/O and are very sensitive to overvoltage. Customers will still need to support legacy 1.8V and 3.3V protocols on these devices without reliability degradation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Supporting legacy voltages on advanced nodes is a growing technical bottleneck that favors specialist I/O IP vendors.

insights.claim: Certus Semiconductor says it has designed 3.3V-to-5V-tolerant I/O in 1.8V FinFET processes and has developed circuit topologies that extend the life of I/O devices running at high I/O voltages.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This is the capability claim behind Certus's positioning for advanced-node I/O.
